title: Notification System: Complete Architecture
description: Design an enterprise multi-channel notification platform (Push, SMS, Email, In-App) with priority queues, rate limiting, and batch digests.

data.text: Design a high-scale, centralized notification platform capable of delivering billions of messages daily across four major delivery channels: Mobile Push (Apple APNs / Google FCM), SMS (Twilio / AWS SNS), Email (SendGrid / Amazon SES), and In-App WebSockets. The system must process critical transactional alerts (e.g. One-Time Passwords, security logins, fraud alerts) with sub-second delivery while handling bulk marketing blasts, respecting per-user channel preferences and quiet hours, deduplicating repetitive alerts, and preventing notification fatigue.

terms.definition: Segregating high-priority transactional notifications (OTP, fraud, order confirmations) into dedicated expedited queues separate from low-priority marketing campaigns.
Collapsing multiple related events into a single batched notification (e.g. "Alice and 4 others liked your post") over a sliding time window.
A rule engine evaluating user opt-outs, channel routing rules, and local timezone quiet hours (e.g. suppress non-critical push alerts between 10 PM and 8 AM).
A unique token derived from `hash(user_id + event_type + entity_id)` cached in Redis for 10-60 minutes to prevent sending duplicate notifications upon upstream retries.
Ingesting status callbacks from downstream providers (delivered, bounced, rejected, marked as spam) to maintain sender reputation and delivery audit trails.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Multi-Channel Dispatch: Route notifications across Mobile Push (iOS/Android), SMS, Email, and In-App WebSockets
Dynamic Template Engine: Render localized templates with parameter interpolation (e.g. "Hello {{name}}, your order #{{id}} is on the way")
User Preference Engine: Respect category subscriptions (Marketing, Security, Social) and channel priority
Quiet Hours Enforcement: Automatically queue or defer non-urgent messages during the recipient's nighttime window
Event Aggregation / Digests: Merge high-frequency social events within a 15-minute sliding window into a single message
Delivery Tracking & Analytics: Ingest provider delivery callbacks (sent, delivered, opened, clicked, bounced)

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Scale: 100M+ notifications sent daily; peak throughput of 100,000 notifications/sec
Latency SLA: Sub-2 seconds end-to-end delivery for High-Priority transactional alerts (OTP / 2FA)
Reliability: At-least-once delivery guarantee across all channels with automatic exponential retry
Deduplication: Guarantee zero duplicate notifications sent within a 10-minute duplicate window
Provider Agility: Automatic failover between secondary providers (e.g. Twilio -> MessageBird on SMS outage)

data.text: The architecture decouples internal client microservices from downstream third-party delivery vendors via an asynchronous priority queue backbone. A central Notification Engine handles validation, deduplication, preference evaluation, and templating before assigning jobs to channel-specific worker pools.

faqs.question: How do you prevent duplicate notifications when the network glitches?
faqs.answer: Derive a deterministic `Idempotency-Key` from the event payload: `SHA256(user_id + notification_type + entity_id + window_hour)`. When an API request arrives, execute `SETNX key 1 EX 600` in Redis. If the key already exists, return HTTP 200 OK immediately and drop the duplicate request, ensuring upstream service retries never send duplicate SMS or emails.

faqs.question: Why use separate queues for High-Priority vs Bulk notifications?
faqs.answer: If a marketing team triggers a 5-million-user newsletter blast at 10:00 AM, a shared queue would fill with 5 million low-priority jobs. A user attempting to log in would wait 15 minutes for their two-factor OTP code to process. Dedicated P0 queues ensure transactional alerts bypass marketing queues and consume dedicated worker pools with 0ms wait.

faqs.question: How are provider outages handled without dropped notifications?
faqs.answer: Third-party providers (e.g. Twilio) periodically suffer regional degradations. Notification worker adapters use a Circuit Breaker pattern. If consecutive provider failures exceed 5%, the circuit trips open, and traffic automatically routes to an active standby secondary provider (e.g. MessageBird / AWS SNS) while alerts notify the on-call engineer.

faqs.question: How does Event Aggregation (Digests) work in practice?
faqs.answer: When a non-urgent social event occurs (e.g. "User liked your comment"), the engine checks if the user has an open aggregation window. If yes, it appends the actor ID to a Redis list (`digest:user_id:likes`). A background timer (15 minutes) drains the list, counts the unique actors, and dispatches a single composite push: "John and 4 others liked your comment".

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Priority queues strictly isolate urgent transactional alerts (OTP) from massive marketing email blasts
Deterministic idempotency keys in Redis eliminate duplicate sends caused by upstream network retries
Provider circuit breakers automatically fail over to secondary vendors when primary gateways degrade
Sliding-window aggregation buffers high-frequency social events to prevent user notification fatigue
Delivery webhook collectors log receipt, bounce, and spam metrics into analytical stores for reputation audit
data.takeaway: Scalable notification systems safeguard user experience through strict priority routing and deduplication, orchestrating multi-channel delivery while respecting personal quiet hours and preferences.
